To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b401109bb512f5ad13ccef3346fd3cf2c51eb70eced978aa995f3db597408196.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=y\,⟹\,y=x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
z=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,x\le y\le \sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/2393b79260273fa658f846ed9013156dbc280195b8d7a0e9b0aeca6cd46e545d.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=x \\ y=\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,⟹\,z=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/f14c08f7d809bbb9eb83dc6f34bfd69ed93963c5dab219d7e6fb16720204ae61.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $z,$ then $x,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.problem:
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz=$

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$*
after.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(y,z),$ ${u}_{2}(y,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\frac{z}{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le x\le \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\,\,\sqrt{x}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2}}
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/29c722bce3c23c2af628f18dfaf16695f9ec5beac68b0d16ce93d6a993d6fb8c.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\sqrt{x}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/cdc8fb2c7f6ef9a28b01094ef3bf18089297a6ef9a431c5152311e5e92cd2557.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type II region and its projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $x$-axis and in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/d805df26c5a471323d855194b41e052142e711e7f7f9ddf910d792ae74cbc2c6.png)

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

- The back boundary of the region is

$$
x=0.
$$

- The front boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y,z),$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{x}\,⟹\,x={y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/4d40e420abeec633cd145dca33071d6459e4b4009e4c6cfc871d6c6150be51e4.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $yz$-plane with the left curve given by $y=\sqrt{0}=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/81782a6c847e5369dfed7524619de354ff7676a856685fb4340d09cf61dca339.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dx\,dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}{[y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{y})]}_{x=0}^{x={y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-0)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\,\text{d}z]\cdot [{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y] \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}-0)\cdot (-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

∫0π/2∫0π2/4∫xπ/2zycos⁡(xy)dydxdz=

Hint: Change the order of integration to dxdydz.

a
2π23
b
π2−1
c
π28
d
3π1
e
3π−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration u1(y,z), u2(y,z), v1(z), v2(z), a, and b such that ∫0π/2∫0π2/4∫xπ/2zycos⁡(xy)dydxdz=∫ab∫v1(z)v2(z)∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)zycos⁡(xy)dxdydz

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration R can be written as a type III region as follows: R={(x,y,z):0≤z≤π2,0≤x≤π24,x≤y≤π2}

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the xz-plane, given by E={(x,z):0≤x≤π24,0≤z≤π2} as shown below.

Then, the region R is shown in the diagram below, where x≤y≤π2.

To change the order of integration from dydxdz to dxdydz, we write R as a type II region and its projection D onto the yz-plane as a type II plane region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the x-axis and in the direction of increasing x, as shown below.

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

  • The back boundary of the region is x=0.

  • The front boundary of the region, written in the form x=x(y,z), is y=x⟹x=y2.

Therefore, the type II representation of R is R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤y2},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type II plane region in the yz-plane with the left curve given by y=0=0.

Hence, D={(y,z):0≤y≤π2,0≤z≤π2}.

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain ∫0π/2∫0π2/4∫xπ/2zycos⁡(xy)dydxdz=∫0π/2∫0π/2∫0y2zycos⁡(xy)dxdydz=∫0π/2∫0π/2zy[∫0y2cos⁡(xy)dx]dydz=∫0π/2∫0π/2zy[ysin⁡(xy)]x=0x=y2dydz=∫0π/2∫0π/2zy(ysin⁡y−0)dydz=∫0π/2∫0π/2zsin⁡ydydz=[∫0π/2zdz]⋅[∫0π/2sin⁡ydy]=[12z2]0π/2⋅[−cos⁡y]0π/2=12⋅(π24−0)⋅(−0+1)=π28.

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration
content.problem:
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz=$

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$*
content.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(y,z),$ ${u}_{2}(y,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\frac{z}{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le x\le \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\,\,\sqrt{x}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2}}
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/29c722bce3c23c2af628f18dfaf16695f9ec5beac68b0d16ce93d6a993d6fb8c.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\sqrt{x}\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/cdc8fb2c7f6ef9a28b01094ef3bf18089297a6ef9a431c5152311e5e92cd2557.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type II region and its projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $x$-axis and in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/d805df26c5a471323d855194b41e052142e711e7f7f9ddf910d792ae74cbc2c6.png)

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

- The back boundary of the region is

$$
x=0.
$$

- The front boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y,z),$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{x}\,⟹\,x={y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/4d40e420abeec633cd145dca33071d6459e4b4009e4c6cfc871d6c6150be51e4.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $yz$-plane with the left curve given by $y=\sqrt{0}=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/81782a6c847e5369dfed7524619de354ff7676a856685fb4340d09cf61dca339.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{\pi }^{2}/4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\frac{z}{y}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,dx\,dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{y})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}{[y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{y})]}_{x=0}^{x={y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{z}{y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-0)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}z\,\text{d}z]\cdot [{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y] \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}-0)\cdot (-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/380b44a8baf8ed15eb3eb4e66e77b820f5bc51a73be840526db67d96f6d763ed.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.$*
after.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}y}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/185f85445f95382afdd9516351f0cce3c4d2b11d99f65da2d5a36db0fc853215.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/6aeba17b071bd275be7147ffb925b488881a2fb8de5f544dbffe8caab5c036e4.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}y\,⟹\,y=2x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=2.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,2x\le y\le 2},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/be089ef60080ad9181db8a5dacccf6abe382bef492369342fa15761134b507d2.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by $x=\frac{1}{2}(2)=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/885b884fee574cae3c2f62ac0092e64b9be1731ae8510f6e910d0a101ffa3f20.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dy\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[{\int }_{2x}^{2}\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2-2x}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2(1-x)}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[z]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}y}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/185f85445f95382afdd9516351f0cce3c4d2b11d99f65da2d5a36db0fc853215.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/6aeba17b071bd275be7147ffb925b488881a2fb8de5f544dbffe8caab5c036e4.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}y\,⟹\,y=2x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=2.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,2x\le y\le 2},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/be089ef60080ad9181db8a5dacccf6abe382bef492369342fa15761134b507d2.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by $x=\frac{1}{2}(2)=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/885b884fee574cae3c2f62ac0092e64b9be1731ae8510f6e910d0a101ffa3f20.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dy\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[{\int }_{2x}^{2}\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2-2x}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2(1-x)}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[z]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$
The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*
after.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{y}\le z\le 1}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/30e43d707479d17f45fb74c023d16706ba9308ffc4421cb17a23d7c2ef16fbee.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/4429082d4ab0d6fdef75d79b1db02944f0c53741fb0ccf19d8a4ef46a253698f.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=(x,z),$ is

$$
z=\sqrt{y}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}
$$

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le {z}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/a941e1bfabb21561b622080775c3c5389a86cf4150f1fb28dd692a022f607620.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by $z=\sqrt{1}=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/20e339260b0947f92d8fedfa47e899ed53753e03e30c4b816edec06d092d9a01.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}{[y]}_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}\,{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}\,{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{e}^{{z}^{3}}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{e-1}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e-1}{3}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{e-1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration u1(x,z), u2(x,z), v1(x), v2(x), a, and b such that

∫01∫01∫y1ez3dzdydx=∫ab∫v1(x)v2(x)∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)ez3dydzdx

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration R can be written as a type I region as follows:

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1,y≤z≤1}

The region R is shown below.

To change the order of integration from dzdydx to dydzdx, we write R as a type III region and its projection D onto the xz-plane as a type I plane region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the y-axis and in the direction of increasing y, as shown below.

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

  • The right boundary of the region, written in the form y=(x,z), is z=y⟹y=z2

  • The left boundary of the region is y=0.

Therefore, the type III representation of R is

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,0≤y≤z2},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the xz-plane with the top curve given by z=1=1.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤1}.

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

∫01∫01∫y1ez3dzdydx=∫01∫01∫0z2ez3dydzdx=∫01∫01ez3[∫0z2dy]dzdx=∫01∫01ez3[y]0z2dzdx=∫01∫01z2ez3dzdx=∫01[∫01z2ez3dz]dx=∫01[ez33]01dx=∫01e−13dx=e−13[x]01=e−13.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/8ac5fd57665f292d8a013f47aaf20226944315bb1f74695e895dca40332b28c6.png)

Evaluate
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$
The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*
content.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{y}\le z\le 1}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/30e43d707479d17f45fb74c023d16706ba9308ffc4421cb17a23d7c2ef16fbee.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/4429082d4ab0d6fdef75d79b1db02944f0c53741fb0ccf19d8a4ef46a253698f.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=(x,z),$ is

$$
z=\sqrt{y}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}
$$

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le {z}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/a941e1bfabb21561b622080775c3c5389a86cf4150f1fb28dd692a022f607620.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by $z=\sqrt{1}=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/20e339260b0947f92d8fedfa47e899ed53753e03e30c4b816edec06d092d9a01.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{z}^{3}}{[y]}_{0}^{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}\,{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}\,{e}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{e}^{{z}^{3}}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{e-1}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{e-1}{3}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{e-1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Reordering gives 0≤y≤√π and 0≤z≤√y. Integrating over z yields (y/2)cos(π/6+y²). Its integral is [sin(π/6+y²)/4]₀^{√π}=(−1/2−1/2)/4=−1/4. The x interval has length 1.

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/3bb477b93fb92174307bee87130d9957b135cdafaa4167f78f3d603c4192391d.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where ${z}^{2}\le y\le \sqrt{\pi }.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/cf966e9ec5fbcf11727d46bb3906f05e4b30df4c9bef86a6eab4850b967d7ba0.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/88b5e19c3e263d160db8d041fd3504b25d4a8a8f7ae8e111cdeb5b153c3cd21f.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y={z}^{2}\,⟺\,z=\sqrt{y}.
$$

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

$$

$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b748578888fdda878b0d44bb036310644c3437c1922aafd49cab6c165a9cf132.png)

EXPLANATION

We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration u1(x,y), u2(x,y), v1(x), v2(x), a, and b such that

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration R can be written as a type III region as follows:

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤π4,z2≤y≤π}

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the xz-plane, given by E={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤π4}

as shown below.

Then, the region R is shown in the diagram below, where z2≤y≤π.

To change the order of integration from dydzdx to dzdydx, we write R as a type I region and its projection D onto the xy-plane as a type I plane region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the z-axis and in the direction of increasing z, as shown below.

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

  • The top boundary of the region, written in the form z=z(x,y), is y=z2⟺z=y.

  • The bottom boundary of the region is z=0.

Therefore, the type I representation of R is

R={(x,y,z):(x,y)∈D,0≤z≤y},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the xy-plane with the top curve given by y=π.

Hence, D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤π}.

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

∫01∫0π4∫z2πzcos⁡(π6+y2)dydzdx=∫01∫0π∫0yzcos⁡(π6+y2)dzdydx=∫01∫0πcos⁡(π6+y2)[∫0yzdz]dydx=∫01∫0πcos⁡(π6+y2)[z22]0ydydx=∫01∫0πy2cos⁡(π6+y2)dydx=∫01[∫0πy2cos⁡(π6+y2)dy]dx=∫01[14sin⁡(π6+y2)]0πdx=∫0114(sin⁡(7π6)−sin⁡(π6))dx=∫01−14dx=[−x4]01=−14.

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt[4]{\pi },\,\,{z}^{2}\le y\le \sqrt{\pi }}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt[4]{\pi }}
$$

as shown below.

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where ${z}^{2}\le y\le \sqrt{\pi }.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/cf966e9ec5fbcf11727d46bb3906f05e4b30df4c9bef86a6eab4850b967d7ba0.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/88b5e19c3e263d160db8d041fd3504b25d4a8a8f7ae8e111cdeb5b153c3cd21f.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y={z}^{2}\,⟺\,z=\sqrt{y}.
$$

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b748578888fdda878b0d44bb036310644c3437c1922aafd49cab6c165a9cf132.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xy$-plane with the top curve given by $y=\sqrt{\pi }.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/60e35d0e77314aaecc60b0eda3c039afa0bdd44d49f68ad39e27c8856a9390e0.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{\pi }}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}z\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}z\,\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2}){[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\frac{y}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\frac{y}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}+{y}^{2})]}_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}))\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{x}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/446e61491ae43e610dc39e4b46b752668969540f7733bf7d9c945fa260210a77.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*
after.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le z\le 1}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b486ea542dc330a483fa76f333ab80c9fcd07434db5dc0c5a0a62a335294f127.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b626c20c336bc81df9194f161998f7c6aea524a11495fede615cdf76f5d93f59.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
z=y\,⟹\,y=z.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le z},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/7386453aebec047469c829e2c2c5d6c4ab915ac965bbcd39838dc7be50941d54.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the bottom curve given by $z=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/4b2bb3583b5c0807c653f503cdf9ed954f38db8a30eef548738e96cedb889288.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{z}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{z}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}z\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{3}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{z}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{z}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}z\sqrt{1-{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{3}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
